domanda: Contoso hosts the public DNS zone contoso.com in Azure DNS. An administrator attempts to create a record set with the relative name @ so that requests for contoso.com are redirected to the name webfarm.contoso.net. The operation fails. Which record type is the administrator attempting to create that the DNS standards do not permit at the zone apex?
spiegazione: CNAME is correct. Because the zone apex (name = @) always contains the NS and SOA record sets that are created automatically with the zone, a CNAME record set cannot coexist with them. CNAME record sets cannot coexist with any other record set of the same name, so a CNAME can never be created at the zone apex. This constraint comes from the DNS standards, not from Azure DNS. TXT is wrong because TXT record sets are fully supported at the zone apex and are routinely used there for SPF and domain-verification values. MX is wrong because MX record sets at the apex are the normal way to publish mail servers for a domain and are supported. A is wrong because an A record set at the apex is supported and is the standard way to point a naked domain at an IPv4 address; an A record set can also be qualified as an alias record set at the apex.

domanda: Your company purchased the domain adatum.com from a third-party domain registrar. You create a public DNS zone named adatum.com in Azure DNS and add the required A and MX record sets. Internet clients still cannot resolve names in adatum.com. What must you do to complete the delegation of the domain to Azure DNS?
opzione_a: At the domain registrar, replace the existing name server records for adatum.com with the Azure DNS name servers assigned to the zone.
opzione_b: In the adatum.com zone in Azure DNS, modify the host property of the SOA record set to reference the registrar's name servers.
opzione_c: In the adatum.com zone in Azure DNS, remove the prepopulated Azure DNS name servers from the apex NS record set and add the registrar's name servers.
opzione_d: At the domain registrar, create a CNAME record that maps adatum.com to the first Azure DNS name server assigned to the zone.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. Azure DNS is an authoritative DNS service, not a domain registrar. Delegation is performed in the parent zone: you take the four Azure DNS name servers that were assigned to your zone and configure them as the NS records for the domain at your registrar. Until the registrar publishes those NS records, recursive resolvers never reach Azure DNS. Option B is wrong because the SOA host property is preconfigured by Azure DNS to the primary name server it provides and is the one SOA property you cannot modify; changing SOA would not affect delegation anyway. Option C is wrong because removing or modifying the prepopulated Azure DNS name servers in the apex NS record set is not allowed, and the authoritative NS records inside the child zone do not perform the delegation - the records in the parent zone do. Option D is wrong because delegation is done with NS records, not CNAME records, and a CNAME cannot exist at the zone apex in any case.

domanda: A storage account is configured with a private endpoint for the blob subresource. Which private DNS zone name must be used so that the private endpoint DNS zone configuration is generated automatically in the Azure public cloud?
spiegazione: Option A is correct. For a storage account private endpoint with the blob or blob_secondary subresource in the Azure public cloud, the recommended private DNS zone name is privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, with blob.core.windows.net as the public DNS zone forwarder. Private endpoint private DNS zone configurations are only generated automatically when this recommended naming scheme is used. Option B is wrong because privatelink.web.core.windows.net corresponds to the web and web_secondary subresources (static website endpoint), not blob. Option C is wrong because privatelink.storage.azure.com is not a recommended zone name for any storage subresource; Microsoft builds privatelink zones by prefixing privatelink to the existing public suffix. Option D is wrong because the privatelink label must be the leftmost label of the zone name - the correct form is privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, not blob.privatelink.core.windows.net.
tags: private dns zone,private endpoint,storage account,blob,zone naming

domanda: Fabrikam runs a web application behind an Azure Traffic Manager profile named fabweb.trafficmanager.net that contains only external endpoints. The public DNS zone fabrikam.com is hosted in Azure DNS. Users must be able to reach the application by browsing to https://fabrikam.com, and the DNS configuration must not require manual updates if the underlying endpoints change. What should you create in the fabrikam.com zone?
opzione_a: A CNAME record set named @ that targets fabweb.trafficmanager.net
opzione_b: An A record set named @ that is qualified as an alias record set targeting the Traffic Manager profile
opzione_c: An A record set named @ that contains the IPv4 address currently returned by fabweb.trafficmanager.net
opzione_d: An NS record set named @ that contains fabweb.trafficmanager.net
spiegazione: Option B is correct. Alias record sets are supported for the A, AAAA, and CNAME record types and, unlike CNAME records, they can be created at the zone apex. An A alias record set pointing to a Traffic Manager profile lets you host a load-balanced application at the naked domain, and Azure DNS resolves the record dynamically so no manual maintenance is required. This works when the Traffic Manager profile contains only external endpoints, which is stated in the scenario. Option A is wrong because the DNS protocol prevents CNAME records at the zone apex - this is precisely the limitation that alias records exist to solve. Option C is wrong because it hard-codes an address that is not guaranteed to remain stable, producing a dangling DNS record and defeating the requirement to avoid manual updates. Option D is wrong because the apex NS record set is created and managed automatically by Azure DNS, cannot have its prepopulated name servers removed, and NS records delegate a zone rather than resolve an application name.
tags: azure dns,alias record,zone apex,traffic manager,public zone

domanda: A virtual network named VNet1 is already linked to a private DNS zone named corp.contoso.internal with autoregistration enabled. A colleague creates a second private DNS zone named apps.contoso.internal and attempts to create a virtual network link from that zone to VNet1 with autoregistration enabled. The operation fails. What is the cause, and what is the supported way to link VNet1 to apps.contoso.internal?
opzione_a: A virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone in total. VNet1 must be unlinked from corp.contoso.internal first.
opzione_b: A virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone with autoregistration enabled. Create the link to apps.contoso.internal without autoregistration.
opzione_c: Autoregistration requires the virtual network and the private DNS zone to be in the same resource group. Move apps.contoso.internal to the resource group of VNet1.
opzione_d: A private DNS zone can have only one registration virtual network. Create a second private DNS zone with the same name in another resource group and link VNet1 to it.
spiegazione: Option B is correct. A specific virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone when automatic registration is enabled - that zone becomes the registration zone for the virtual network. Linking VNet1 to apps.contoso.internal without autoregistration makes it a resolution virtual network, and a virtual network can have many resolution zones associated with it, so records in apps.contoso.internal will still resolve from VNet1. Option A is wrong because a virtual network can be linked to up to 1,000 private DNS zones; only the autoregistration link is limited to one. Option C is wrong because there is no same-resource-group requirement - a private DNS zone can be linked to virtual networks in other resource groups, subscriptions, and even other tenants, given write permissions on both objects. Option D is wrong because a private DNS zone can have multiple registration virtual networks; the restriction runs the other way. Creating duplicate zones would not lift the one-registration-zone-per-virtual-network limit.
tags: private dns zone,virtual network link,autoregistration,registration zone,resolution zone

domanda: A private endpoint is deployed in VNet1 for a storage account, and the private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net contains the correct A record and is linked to VNet1. Virtual machines in VNet1 resolve the storage account FQDN to the private IP address as expected. Virtual machines in VNet2, which is peered with VNet1 and uses the default Azure-provided DNS settings, still resolve the FQDN to the public IP address of the storage account. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a virtual network link between the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone and VNet2.
opzione_b: Enable the Allow gateway transit option on the peering from VNet1 to VNet2.
opzione_c: Create a second private endpoint for the storage account in VNet2.
opzione_d: Enable autoregistration on the existing virtual network link between the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone and VNet1.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. DNS resolution against a private DNS zone works only from virtual networks that are linked to that zone. Virtual network peering does not propagate private DNS zone resolution, so VNet2 falls through to public DNS and receives the public IP. Creating a virtual network link from the zone to VNet2 makes VNet2 a resolution virtual network and lets its VMs resolve the privatelink record. Option B is wrong because gateway transit controls whether a peered network can use the other network's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway; it has no effect on private DNS zone resolution. Option C is wrong because it is unnecessary and adds cost - the existing private endpoint is already reachable from VNet2 over the peering; only name resolution is missing. Option D is wrong because autoregistration only creates A records for virtual machines deployed in the linked virtual network. It does nothing for private endpoint records and would not affect resolution from VNet2; the zone also cannot be a registration zone for a network it is not linked to.
tags: private dns zone,virtual network link,private endpoint,peering,troubleshooting

domanda: VNet1 is linked to a private DNS zone named db.contoso.internal. The DNS servers setting of VNet1 was changed from Default (Azure-provided) to a custom DNS server that runs on a domain controller virtual machine inside VNet1. After the change, virtual machines in VNet1 can no longer resolve records in db.contoso.internal. You must restore resolution while keeping the custom DNS server for Active Directory name resolution. What should you do on the domain controller?
opzione_a: Configure a conditional forwarder for db.contoso.internal that points to 168.63.129.16.
opzione_b: Configure a root hint that points to the four Azure DNS name servers assigned to the private DNS zone.
opzione_c: Create a secondary zone for db.contoso.internal and configure a zone transfer from Azure Private DNS.
opzione_d: Configure a conditional forwarder for db.contoso.internal that points to the first IP address of the VNet1 address space.
spiegazione: Option A is correct. When you define a custom DNS server on a virtual network, the custom setting overrides the default name resolution order and the system no longer automatically queries the private DNS zones linked to that virtual network. If the custom DNS server is a virtual machine, you must configure a conditional forwarder for the private zone that points to Azure DNS at the well-known virtual IP address 168.63.129.16. (Alternatively, an Azure DNS Private Resolver in a linked virtual network can be used as the forwarding target.) Option B is wrong because Azure Private DNS zones are not resolvable from the public DNS hierarchy and are not served by the public Azure DNS name servers, so root hints cannot reach them. Option C is wrong because Azure Private DNS does not expose zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR); you cannot stand up a secondary copy of a private zone. Option D is wrong because the correct target is the Azure DNS virtual IP 168.63.129.16, not an address derived from the virtual network address space; the first usable addresses of a subnet are reserved by Azure but do not host the recursive resolver.

domanda: You are designing DNS records in a public Azure DNS zone and want to use alias record sets wherever they are supported. Which targets can an alias record set in an Azure DNS zone reference? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A Standard SKU public IP address resource
opzione_d: The private IP configuration of a virtual machine network interface
opzione_e: The fully qualified domain name of an on-premises web server
spiegazione: A, B, and C are correct. Azure DNS alias record sets (supported for the A, AAAA, and CNAME types) can point to a Standard SKU public IP resource, to a Traffic Manager profile, to an Azure Content Delivery Network endpoint, to an Azure Front Door endpoint, or to another DNS record set of the same type within the same zone. Coupling the record's life cycle to the Azure resource is what prevents dangling DNS records and updates the record automatically when the target IP changes or the target is deleted. Option D is wrong because alias records reference Azure resources such as public IP resources, not private IP configurations on a network interface; a public DNS zone is also the wrong place to publish private addresses. Option E is wrong because alias records must reference an Azure resource or another record set in the same zone - an arbitrary external FQDN is not a supported alias target and would be expressed as a normal (non-alias) CNAME record.
tags: azure dns,alias record,public ip,traffic manager,front door,dangling dns

domanda: Your organization plans to consolidate internal name resolution onto a single Azure Private DNS zone that is shared by workloads in several subscriptions and regions. Which statements about Azure Private DNS zones are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A single private DNS zone can be linked to virtual networks that are located in different Azure regions.
opzione_b: Virtual networks must be peered with each other before records in a shared private DNS zone can resolve across them.
opzione_c: A virtual network that belongs to a different Azure subscription can be linked to the private DNS zone.
opzione_d: You can create NS record sets in a private DNS zone to delegate a child domain to another private DNS zone.
opzione_e: When a linked virtual network is deleted, its virtual network links and autoregistered DNS records are removed automatically.
spiegazione: A, C, and E are correct. Private DNS zone data is stored as a global resource, so the same zone can be linked to virtual networks in multiple regions and remains available if one virtual network or region is affected. A virtual network in a different subscription (or even a different tenant) can be linked as long as you have write permission on both the virtual network and the private DNS zone. When you delete a linked virtual network, the virtual network links and the autoregistered DNS records associated with it are cleared automatically - no manual unlink is required. Option B is wrong because forward DNS resolution across virtual networks linked to the same private zone has no dependency on peering; you may peer networks for data-plane traffic, but resolution does not require it. Option D is wrong because you cannot create zone delegations (NS records) in a private DNS zone. If you need a child domain, you create it directly as its own private DNS zone and link it to the virtual network.
tags: private dns zone,virtual network link,cross-subscription,ns delegation,autoregistration

domanda: Litware is deploying private endpoints in the Azure public cloud for an Azure Key Vault, an Azure SQL Database logical server, and an Azure App Service web app. The private DNS zone configuration for each private endpoint must be generated automatically, so the recommended zone names must be used. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Private DNS zone for the Key Vault private endpoint (vault subresource): [privatelink.vault.azure.net | privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net | privatelink.keyvault.azure.net]
opzione_b: Private DNS zone for the Azure SQL Database private endpoint (sqlServer subresource): [privatelink.database.windows.net | privatelink.sql.azure.com | privatelink.sqlserver.windows.net]
opzione_c: Private DNS zone for the App Service private endpoint (sites subresource): [privatelink.azurewebsites.net | privatelink.web.core.windows.net | privatelink.appservice.azure.com]
opzione_d: Record type that Azure creates in the private DNS zone for each private endpoint: [A | CNAME | SRV]
spiegazione: For Azure Key Vault (Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults, vault subresource) the recommended private DNS zone in the public cloud is privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net, with vault.azure.net and vaultcore.azure.net as the public DNS zone forwarders; privatelink.vault.azure.net and privatelink.keyvault.azure.net are not recommended zone names and would prevent the private DNS zone configuration from being generated automatically. For Azure SQL Database (Microsoft.Sql/servers, sqlServer subresource) the zone is privatelink.database.windows.net, derived from the public suffix database.windows.net; privatelink.sql.azure.com and privatelink.sqlserver.windows.net do not exist. For Azure Web Apps and Function Apps (Microsoft.Web/sites, sites subresource) the zone is privatelink.azurewebsites.net; privatelink.web.core.windows.net belongs to the storage account static website subresource and privatelink.appservice.azure.com is not a recommended zone. Azure creates an A record in the privatelink zone that maps the resource name to the private endpoint's private IP address - the CNAME is what Azure publishes in the public DNS to redirect resolution into the privatelink namespace, and SRV records are not used by private endpoints.
tags: private dns zone,private endpoint,zone naming,key vault,azure sql,app service

domanda: You administer the public DNS zone northwind.com in Azure DNS and must document how record sets behave in the zone. Select the appropriate option to complete each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum number of records that a single CNAME record set can contain: [1 | 20 | 400]
opzione_b: Record type that must be used to publish Sender Policy Framework information: [SPF | TXT | CAA]
opzione_c: Record type used to specify which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain: [CAA | CNAME | TLSA]
opzione_d: Record set type that can be created at the zone apex to reference a Traffic Manager profile: [CNAME | A alias | NS]
spiegazione: The DNS standards do not permit multiple records with the same name for the SOA and CNAME types, so a CNAME record set can contain only a single record. The value 20 is the general limit on records per record set in a public zone, and 400 is the limit for TXT records per record set - neither applies to CNAME. SPF information must be published using the TXT record type: RFC 7208 deprecated the dedicated SPF record type, and Azure DNS does not support it; when a zone file is imported, SPF-type records are converted to TXT. CAA is the record type that lets domain owners declare which certificate authorities are authorized to issue certificates, using the flags, tag (issue, issuewild, iodef), and value properties; CNAME is an aliasing record and TLSA associates a TLS certificate or public key with a name and requires DNSSEC. Finally, a CNAME cannot exist at the zone apex, and the apex NS record set is reserved and managed by Azure DNS, so an A record set qualified as an alias record set is the supported way to point the apex at a Traffic Manager profile.

domanda: A hub-and-spoke deployment will share one Azure Private DNS zone across a large number of spoke virtual networks. Before submitting a design review, you must record the default service limits that apply. Select the appropriate value to complete each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum number of virtual network links per private DNS zone: [100 | 1000 | 25000]
opzione_b: Maximum number of virtual network links with autoregistration enabled per private DNS zone: [1 | 100 | 1000]
opzione_c: Maximum number of private DNS zones that a single virtual network can be linked to with autoregistration enabled: [1 | 100 | 1000]
spiegazione: The default Azure DNS limits for private DNS zones are: 1,000 virtual network links per private DNS zone; 100 virtual network links per private DNS zone with autoregistration enabled; and 1 private DNS zone that a given virtual network can be linked to with autoregistration enabled. The distractors are real Azure DNS limits taken from adjacent rows of the same table, which is what makes them plausible: 100 is the autoregistration link limit per zone (not the total link limit), 25,000 is the maximum number of record sets per private DNS zone, and 1,000 is both the total virtual network links per zone and the number of private DNS zones a virtual network can be linked to without autoregistration - but only one of those links may be a registration link. The one-registration-zone-per-virtual-network rule is the design constraint that most often forces a separate resolution-only zone in hub-and-spoke topologies.
tags: private dns zone,limits,virtual network link,autoregistration,hub and spoke

domanda: VNet1 is linked to a private DNS zone named ops.contoso.internal, and autoregistration is enabled on the link. VNet1 contains a virtual machine named VM1 that has two network interfaces, NIC1 (primary) and NIC2 (secondary), each with a private IP address. VNet1 also contains an internal load balancer named ILB1 that has a static private IP address in a subnet of VNet1. Evaluate each of the following statements. 1. An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC1 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal. 2. An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC2 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal. 3. If VM1 is stopped and deallocated, the autoregistered DNS record for VM1 is removed from ops.contoso.internal.
opzione_a: An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC1 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal.
opzione_b: An A record for VM1 that maps to the private IP address of NIC2 is created automatically in ops.contoso.internal.
opzione_c: If VM1 is stopped and deallocated, the autoregistered DNS record for VM1 is removed from ops.contoso.internal.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. When a virtual network link has autoregistration enabled, Azure DNS creates an address (A) record for each virtual machine deployed in that virtual network, pointing to its private IP address. Statement 2 is No. DNS records are created automatically only for the primary virtual machine NIC. If a virtual machine has more than one NIC, you must create the DNS records for the additional network interfaces manually in the private DNS zone. The same restriction is why no record is created for ILB1 - autoregistration works only for virtual machines, and records for other resources such as internal load balancers must be created manually. Statement 3 is Yes. The autoregistered records track the virtual machine life cycle: records are created when a virtual machine starts in a linked virtual network with autoregistration enabled, and when the virtual machine is stopped and deallocated or deleted, the autoregistered records are removed from the zone.
tags: private dns zone,autoregistration,a record,secondary nic,internal load balancer

domanda: The public domain adatum.com is already delegated to Azure DNS and hosted in a public DNS zone. A separate team must manage the subdomain engineering.adatum.com in its own zone. You plan to create the child zone and the delegation manually, without using the Child zone option in the Azure portal, and then confirm that the delegation resolves. Arrange the actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: In the adatum.com zone, add an NS record set named engineering that contains the name server entries of the child zone.
opzione_b: Create a public DNS zone named engineering.adatum.com in Azure DNS.
opzione_c: Copy the name server names listed in the engineering.adatum.com zone.
opzione_d: Run nslookup www.engineering.adatum.com and confirm that the expected address is returned.
opzione_e: In the engineering.adatum.com zone, create an A record named www that resolves to 10.10.10.10.
spiegazione: The correct order is B, C, A, E, D. First create the child zone engineering.adatum.com in Azure DNS - the parent adatum.com must already exist and already be delegated to Azure DNS, which the scenario states. Creating the child zone causes Azure DNS to assign name servers to it and to populate the authoritative NS record set at the child zone apex, so those name server names can only be copied after the zone exists (C). Next, add an NS record set named engineering to the parent adatum.com zone containing those name server entries (A); setting up the NS records for a child zone in the parent zone is what performs the delegation, and it cannot be done before the child name servers are known. Then create a test record such as the www A record inside the child zone (E) - a record must exist before it can be looked up. Finally, validate the delegation with nslookup for www.engineering.adatum.com (D), which should return a non-authoritative answer of 10.10.10.10. Placing the NS record set before the child zone exists, or testing before the test record is created, produces a delegation that cannot be verified.
